segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Masters, give your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Persevere in prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: praying at the same time for us too, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that I may make it plain, as I ought to speak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Conduct yourselves with wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how you ought to answer each person.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant and fellow slave in the Lord, will tell you all my news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how things are with us and that he may encourage your hearts,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Aristarchus, my fellow captive, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (you have received instructions about him; if he comes to you, welcome him),

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Jesus who is called Justus. Of those from the circumcision, these alone are fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ, greets you. He is always struggling for you in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I can testify of him that he labors hard for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha and the assembly in her house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one from Laodicea.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “See that you fulfill the service you received in the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

notes.note: The Greek word for a slave's 'master' is the same word translated 'Lord' when used of Christ in the preceding verses. Paul's point depends on that identity: slave owners are themselves under a kyrios. English has to choose between 'master' and 'lord', so the wordplay is only partly visible.

notes.traditional: that which is just and equal
notes.note: The second noun can mean 'equality' as well as 'fairness' or 'equity'. Most interpreters take it here as even-handed, equitable treatment rather than a call to treat slaves as social equals, and the translation follows that view. The stronger sense cannot be ruled out.

notes.phrase: making the most of the opportunity
notes.note: The verb is a marketplace word, 'to buy up', and the noun means a particular or opportune time, not time in general. The older rendering 'redeeming the time' suggests rescuing time from something. Most modern translations take the phrase, as here, to mean seizing the present opportunity.

The word is built on the ordinary Greek term for a slave, the same one used of household slaves in verse 1 and of Epaphras in verse 12. 'Servant' is kept in this translation for a different Greek word, which also appears in this verse. Many translations soften both to 'servant'. Paul's language describes belonging to a master, not employment.

This is not Paul's usual word for a prisoner. It means someone taken captive in war. Most translations have 'fellow prisoner'. Whether Aristarchus was literally confined with Paul or the term is a military metaphor for shared hardship in Christ's service is uncertain.

This is a standard way of saying 'Jews', here Jewish believers. Paul is saying that Aristarchus, Mark and Jesus Justus are the only Jewish Christians working alongside him at this time. It follows that Epaphras, Luke and Demas, named next, were Gentiles.

The verb can mean 'fully convinced, assured' or 'filled, brought to completion'. Older translations have 'complete in all the will of God'; many modern ones have 'fully assured'. Either fits a letter much concerned with fullness and with firmness of conviction.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people. It was used for a city's citizen assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or institution. Here the group is one that meets in a private home.

notes.phrase: Nympha and the assembly in her house
notes.traditional: Nymphas, and the church which is in his house
notes.note: The manuscripts differ: some read 'her house' (a woman, Nympha), some 'his house' (a man, Nymphas), and some 'their house'. The name in the Greek text is identical for either gender apart from its accent, which the earliest manuscripts did not write. Most modern editions and translations judge 'her' to be original, with the change to 'his' made by later copyists.

Paul refers to a letter that the Colossians are to obtain from the neighbouring assembly at Laodicea. It is usually thought to be a letter of Paul to the Laodiceans that has not survived. Some scholars identify it with the letter known as Ephesians. A later Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans' is not genuine.

The noun belongs to the same word-family as 'servant' in verse 7 and means a task carried out for another. 'Ministry' is the traditional rendering, but it now suggests a clerical office. What Archippus's assignment was is not known.

notes.traditional: by the hand of me Paul
notes.note: Letters were normally dictated to a scribe. At this point Paul takes the pen and adds a closing line himself, as a sign that the letter is authentic, much as a signature would be. He does the same at the end of several other letters.

candidates.reason: The traditional 'servant' and the literal 'slave' alternate in most translations, and the compound σύνδουλος and titles like 'slave of Christ' must match the rendering used for household slaves.
'Mystery' now suggests a puzzle, whereas the word means a secret God has now disclosed; a single decision between 'mystery' and 'secret' is needed across Paul, the Gospels and Revelation.
The Semitic idiom 'walk' for conduct recurs throughout the letters, and translators split between keeping 'walk' and rendering it 'live' or 'conduct oneself'.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural, of the community); brother (singular, of a named man)
candidates.reason: The plural addressed to mixed communities is rendered 'brothers', 'brethren' or 'brothers and sisters' in different translations and needs one policy.
It is rendered 'perfect', 'mature' or 'complete' by different translators, and the choice affects key passages in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James.
